title: Meet my friend
goal: Introduce other people, choose between *tú* and *usted*, and ask someone's name politely.
bekal: ask what someone else is called
pronounce ll, h, j and ñ correctly

dialogs.title: Diálogo — Presentaciones
dialogs.intro: At a neighborhood event, Ana runs into her much older neighbor and introduces Luis. Notice how the tone changes.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Buenas tardes, señora Gómez. ¿Cómo está usted?
lines.id: Good afternoon, Mrs. Gómez. How are you?
lines.literal: good afternoons, madam Gómez. how are you (polite)?

lines.speaker: Sra. Gómez:
lines.id: Very well, thank you. And you, Ana?
lines.literal: very well, thanks. and you, Ana?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Bien, gracias. Mire, este es mi amigo Luis.
lines.id: Fine, thanks. Look, this is my friend Luis.
lines.literal: well, thanks. look (polite), this is my friend Luis.

lines.speaker: Sra. Gómez:
lines.id: Nice to meet you, Luis. Are you a student too?

lines.speaker: Luis:
lines.text: Sí, señora. Soy estudiante de español.
lines.id: Yes, ma'am. I'm a Spanish student.
lines.literal: yes, madam. am student of Spanish.

lines.speaker: Sra. Gómez:
lines.text: ¡Qué bien! ¿Y cómo se llama tu profesora?
lines.id: How nice! And what's your teacher's name?
lines.literal: how good! and how herself-calls your teacher?

lines.speaker: Luis:
lines.text: Se llama Carmen. Es muy simpática.
lines.id: Her name is Carmen. She's really nice.

lines.speaker: Sra. Gómez:
lines.id: Perfect. Well, see you soon, kids.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.id: Goodbye, Mrs. Gómez. Have a good afternoon!

notes: **Tú or usted?** *Tú* is for friends, peers, family, children, and almost anyone your own age. *Usted* is for people much older than you, bosses, officials, and anyone you don't know in a formal situation. When in doubt, start with *usted*: nobody minds being shown too much respect, and people will usually offer *puedes tutearme* ("you can call me *tú*") themselves.

**Titles.** *Señor* (Mr.), *señora* (Mrs.), *señorita* (Miss, now rarely used for adults). Used with a name, the article appears when you're **talking about** the person — *la señora Gómez es simpática* — but disappears when you're **speaking to** them: *Buenas tardes, señora Gómez*.
**Este es…** = "this is…", used to introduce people. For a woman: *esta es mi amiga Ana*. Notice *mi amigo / mi amiga* — the word for friend follows the gender of the friend, not yours.
**Mire** literally means "look" (polite form), used much like English "look" or "so" — an opener to get the other person's attention. The informal version is *mira*.
**¿Cómo se llama…?** does two jobs: asking a third person's name (*¿cómo se llama tu profesora?*) and asking someone's name politely (*¿cómo se llama usted?*). Context tells you which.
**¡Qué bien!** = "how nice!", one of the exclamations you'll hear most. The pattern is *¡Qué + adjective!* — *¡qué bonito!*, *¡qué difícil!*, *¡qué simpática!*
**Chicos** literally means "boys", but it's used for any mixed group of young people, a bit like "guys" or "you all". An all-female group is *chicas*.

grammars.title: Llamarse (to be called) — a verb with a mirror
body: *Llamarse* literally means "to call oneself". That's why it always comes with a small word in front — *me*, *te*, *se* — pointing back at the person doing it. The small word changes, and so does the verb:
after: So *¿cómo te llamas?* literally means "how do you call yourself?" — not "what is your name". One of the most common beginner mistakes is dropping the small word: *llamo Ana* means nothing; it has to be *me llamo Ana*.
Another way that's just as correct and shorter: *soy Ana*. Both are used every day; *me llamo* is slightly more neutral, *soy* slightly more casual.

blocks.text: Spanish is pronounced almost exactly as it's written — almost. These letters are the ones that trip up English speakers most, and all of them have already appeared in the first two units.

blocks.title: Word stress
items: Words ending in a **vowel, -n or -s** are stressed on the **second-to-last** syllable: *es-tu-**dian**-te*, ***ho**-la*, ***bue**-nos*.
Words ending in any other consonant are stressed on the **last** syllable: *pro-fe-**sor**, us-**ted***.
If there's a ´ over a vowel, it **overrides both rules** — that's where the stress falls: *a-**diós***, *ma-**má***, *tam-**bién***. The mark isn't decoration; *papa* means potato, *papá* means dad.

blocks.title: Two kisses and one long name
items: In Spain, introductions between two women, or a woman and a man, usually come with *dos besos* — two light air kisses, left cheek first. Between men, a handshake is enough. In many Latin American countries it's just **one** kiss. If you're unsure, wait half a second and follow the other person's lead.

Spanish speakers usually have **two surnames**: the first from their father, the second from their mother. *Ana García Morales* is called *señora García*, not *señora Morales*. Married women don't change their surname either.
*Usted* is used far more in Latin America — in Colombia even between friends — while in Spain people switch to *tú* very quickly. Neither is wrong; follow the person in front of you.

exercises.prompt: Fill in *me llamo*, *te llamas* or *se llama*.
Put the words in order to make a correct Spanish sentence.

answers: me llamo — te llamas — se llama — se llama — se llama
¿Cómo te llamas? — Yo soy Luis. — Soy estudiante también. — Este es mi amigo Luis. — No soy profesora.
¡Buenos días! — Me llamo Ana. — Soy estudiante también. — Es profesora. — Muchas gracias. — Hasta mañana.
